## Introduction

Run a Pearson correlation on every brand attribute and you get a tidy ranking: trust looks important, popularity looks fine, move on. Then you fit the full model and half the story changes — because **survey attributes move together**. People who trust a brand also tend to like its design, its service, its social impact. Correlation is not causation, but here it is also not independence.

That is the whole point of **key drivers analysis**: figure out which attributes actually move satisfaction once the others are accounted for. For this optional assignment I built the full comparison table — Pearson, standardized betas, drop-one usefulness, Shapley values, Johnson relative weights, and random-forest Gini importance — on real customer survey data.

The part I enjoyed most: **hand-coding Shapley values** from scratch, using $R^2$ as the fit metric and looping over every predictor subset. With only nine attributes that is manageable; it also makes you feel the method instead of just calling a package.

Here is what I computed for each driver:

1. **Pearson *r*** — bivariate link with satisfaction, no controls
2. **Standardized β** — coefficient in the full linear model
3. **Drop-one usefulness** — how much $R^2$ drops when you remove that predictor
4. **Shapley values** — fair share of $R^2$ (LMG decomposition; my own code)
5. **Johnson relative weights** — orthogonalized $R^2$ shares that sum to the model total
6. **Random forest Gini** — nonlinear importance from 500 trees

Spoiler: the methods mostly agree on the top three. The interesting bit is who *falls* once you stop looking at drivers one at a time.

## The Data

`data_for_drivers_analysis.csv` has **2,553 responses** across two brands. Each row is one person’s yes/no answers to nine attribute statements — trust, build quality, ease of use, social impact, and so on — plus overall **satisfaction** on a 1–5 scale. Binary predictors, ordinal outcome: not glamorous, but very typical of the satisfaction surveys marketers actually run.

```{python}
import base64
import json
import struct
import uuid
from itertools import combinations
from math import factorial
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display
from numpy.linalg import eig, inv

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

DATA_DIR = Path(".")
if not (DATA_DIR / "data_for_drivers_analysis.csv").exists():
    DATA_DIR = Path("blogs/HW5")

DRIVERS = [

ACCENT = "#2e2825"

HIGHLIGHT = "#7a3b35"

pio.templates.default = "simple_white"


def style_axes(ax):
    ax.set_facecolor(PANEL)
    ax.figure.set_facecolor(BG)
    ax.grid(True, axis="both", color=GRID, linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.8)
    for spine in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(colors="#8a8278")
    ax.xaxis.label.set_color(ACCENT)
    ax.yaxis.label.set_color(ACCENT)
    ax.title.set_color(ACCENT)


def _decode_bdata(obj: dict) -> list:
    raw = base64.b64decode(obj["bdata"])
    dtype = obj["dtype"]
    if dtype == "f8":
        return list(struct.unpack(f"<{len(raw) // 8}d", raw))
    if dtype == "f4":
        return list(struct.unpack(f"<{len(raw) // 4}f", raw))
    if dtype == "i2":
        return list(struct.unpack(f"<{len(raw) // 2}h", raw))
    if dtype == "i4":
        return list(struct.unpack(f"<{len(raw) // 4}i", raw))
    return list(raw)


def _plain_json(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        if "bdata" in obj and "dtype" in obj:
            return _decode_bdata(obj)
        return {k: _plain_json(v) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, (list, tuple)):
        return [_plain_json(v) for v in obj]
    if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray):
        return obj.tolist()
    if isinstance(obj, (np.integer, np.floating, np.bool_)):
        return obj.item()
    return obj


def embed_plotly(fig: go.Figure, div_id: str, height: int) -> str:
    fig.update_layout(
        height=height,
        paper_bgcolor=BG,
        plot_bgcolor=PANEL,
        font=dict(color=ACCENT, family="DM Sans, sans-serif"),
    )
    fig.update_xaxes(gridcolor=GRID, zerolinecolor=GRID)
    fig.update_yaxes(gridcolor=GRID, zerolinecolor=GRID)
    raw = fig.to_dict()
    layout = _plain_json(raw.get("layout", {}))
    layout.pop("template", None)
    payload = json.dumps(
        {
            "data": _plain_json(raw.get("data", [])),
            "layout": layout,
            "config": {"displayModeBar": True, "responsive": True},
        }
    )
    return f"""<div id="{div_id}" class="plotly-graph-div" style="width:100%;height:{height}px;"></div>
<script>
(function() {{
  function decodeBdata(obj) {{
    if (Array.isArray(obj)) return obj.map(decodeBdata);
    if (obj && typeof obj === "object") {{
      if (obj.bdata && obj.dtype) {{
        var bin = atob(obj.bdata);
        var buf = new ArrayBuffer(bin.length);
        var view = new Uint8Array(buf);
        for (var i = 0; i < bin.length; i++) view[i] = bin.charCodeAt(i);
        if (obj.dtype === "f8") return Array.from(new Float64Array(buf));
        if (obj.dtype === "f4") return Array.from(new Float32Array(buf));
        if (obj.dtype === "i2") return Array.from(new Int16Array(buf));
        if (obj.dtype === "i4") return Array.from(new Int32Array(buf));
      }}
      var out = {{}};
      for (var k in obj) out[k] = decodeBdata(obj[k]);
      return out;
    }}
    return obj;
  }}
  var spec = decodeBdata({payload});
  function drawPlot() {{
    if (typeof Plotly === "undefined") {{
      setTimeout(drawPlot, 50);
      return;
    }}
    var el = document.getElementById("{div_id}");
    if (!el || el.dataset.plotlyDrawn === "1") return;
    Plotly.newPlot(el, spec.data, spec.layout, spec.config).then(function() {{
      el.dataset.plotlyDrawn = "1";
      if (typeof Plotly.Plots !== "undefined") Plotly.Plots.resize(el);
    }}).catch(function(err) {{
      console.error("Plotly failed ({div_id}):", err);
      el.innerHTML = "<p style='color:#7a3b35;font-size:0.9rem'>Chart could not load — try a hard refresh.</p>";
    }});
  }}
  if (document.readyState === "loading") {{
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", drawPlot);
  }} else {{
    drawPlot();
  }}
}})();
</script>"""


def show_plotly(fig: go.Figure, height=None, caption=None) -> None:
    plot_h = int(height if height is not None else (fig.layout.height or 500))
    div_id = "plot-" + uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]
    html = embed_plotly(fig, div_id, plot_h)
    if caption:
        html += f'<p class="chart-caption"><em>{caption}</em></p>'
    display(HTML(html))


df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "data_for_drivers_analysis.csv")
X = df[DRIVERS].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y = df[OUTCOME].to_numpy(dtype=float)
n, p = X.shape

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "n": [n],
    "brands": [df["brand"].nunique()],
    "mean satisfaction": [df[OUTCOME].mean()],
    "sd satisfaction": [df[OUTCOME].std(ddof=1)],
})
display(Markdown("**Sample overview**"))
display(summary.round(3))
```

## Methods

I standardized satisfaction and all nine attribute dummies, then ran everything off a single multiple regression backbone. Pearson correlations and the random forest are the exceptions — one is purely bivariate, the other deliberately nonlinear.

```{python}
#| echo: true

def r2_subset(indices):
    if not indices:
        return 0.0
    idx = list(indices)
    return LinearRegression().fit(X[:, idx], y).score(X[:, idx], y)


def shapley_r2(values):
    """LMG / Shapley decomposition of R² for linear regression."""
    n_features = values.shape[1]
    shapley = np.zeros(n_features)
    for j in range(n_features):
        others = [i for i in range(n_features) if i != j]
        total = 0.0
        for k in range(len(others) + 1):
            for subset in combinations(others, k):
                subset = list(subset)
                weight = factorial(k) * factorial(n_features - k - 1) / factorial(n_features)
                total += weight * (r2_subset(subset + [j]) - r2_subset(subset))
        shapley[j] = total
    return shapley


def johnson_relative_weights(corr_xx, corr_xy):
    """Johnson's relative weights; raw weights sum to model R²."""
    evals, evecs = eig(corr_xx)
    evals = evals.real
    evecs = evecs.real
    num_x = len(corr_xy)
    diag = np.zeros((num_x, num_x), float)
    diag[np.diag_indices(num_x)] = evals
    delta = np.sqrt(diag)
    coef_xz = evecs @ delta @ evecs.T
    coef_yz = inv(coef_xz) @ corr_xy
    rsquare = np.sum(np.square(coef_yz))
    raw_weights = np.square(coef_xz) @ np.square(coef_yz)
    return raw_weights, rsquare


# Pearson correlations
pearson = np.array([stats.pearsonr(X[:, i], y)[0] for i in range(p)])

# Standardized betas
scaler_x = StandardScaler()
scaler_y = StandardScaler()
x_std = scaler_x.fit_transform(X)
y_std = scaler_y.fit_transform(y.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
full_model = LinearRegression().fit(x_std, y_std)
std_betas = full_model.coef_
full_r2 = full_model.score(x_std, y_std)

# Drop-one usefulness (ΔR²)
drop_one = np.array([full_r2 - r2_subset([j for j in range(p) if j != i]) for i in range(p)])

# Shapley (hand-coded)
shapley = shapley_r2(X)

# Johnson relative weights
corr_all = df[[OUTCOME] + DRIVERS].corr()
corr_xx = corr_all.iloc[1:, 1:].to_numpy()
corr_xy = corr_all.iloc[1:, 0].to_numpy()
johnson_rw, johnson_r2 = johnson_relative_weights(corr_xx, corr_xy)

# Random forest Gini importance
rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X, y)
rf_gini = rf.feature_importances_

display(Markdown(
    f"**Full-model** $R^2 = {full_r2:.3f}$. "
    "Honestly? That is low — most of what drives satisfaction is not in these nine dummies. "
    "But the goal here is *relative* importance among the measured attributes, not explaining everything."
))
```

## Results

The table below is the assignment deliverable: one row per driver, one column per method. Correlations and betas are raw; drop-one, Shapley, and Johnson are **$R^2$ contributions** (together they sum to about 0.109). RF Gini is rescaled to percentages so you can compare it on the same visual scale as the decompositions.

```{python}
#| echo: true

def markdown_table(headers, rows):
    lines = [
        "| " + " | ".join(headers) + " |",
        "| " + " | ".join(["---"] * len(headers)) + " |",
    ]
    for row in rows:
        lines.append("| " + " | ".join(row) + " |")
    return "\n".join(lines)


results = pd.DataFrame({
    "driver": DRIVERS,
    "pearson": pearson,
    "std_beta": std_betas,
    "drop_one": drop_one,
    "shapley": shapley,
    "johnson_rw": johnson_rw,
    "rf_gini": rf_gini,
})
results["johnson_pct"] = results["johnson_rw"] / johnson_r2 * 100
results["rf_gini_pct"] = results["rf_gini"] / results["rf_gini"].sum() * 100
results = results.sort_values("shapley", ascending=False)

rows = []
for _, row in results.iterrows():
    rows.append([
        LABELS[row["driver"]],
        f"{row['pearson']:.3f}",
        f"{row['std_beta']:.3f}",
        f"{row['drop_one']:.4f}",
        f"{row['shapley']:.4f}",
        f"{row['johnson_rw']:.4f}",
        f"{row['johnson_pct']:.1f}%",
        f"{row['rf_gini_pct']:.1f}%",
    ])

display(Markdown(markdown_table(
    [
        "Driver", "Pearson *r*", "Std β", "Drop-one ΔR²",
        "Shapley", "Johnson RW", "Johnson %", "RF Gini %",
    ],
    rows,
)))

display(Markdown(
    f"**Model fit:** $R^2 = {full_r2:.4f}$ "
    f"(Shapley sum = {shapley.sum():.4f}, Johnson sum = {johnson_r2:.4f})"
))
```

## Visualizations

Tables are for precision; charts are for the *oh, that is why* moment. I kept the heatmap static because the labeled cells read better that way. The bar and scatter charts are interactive — hover for exact values, click legend items to toggle methods.

### Driver importance across methods

I rescaled each metric to **percent of its own total** so four different methods fit on one chart. The headline: trust, social impact, and customer service lead everywhere. Popularity and rewarding experience sit at the bottom no matter how you slice it.

```{python}
#| echo: true

plot_df = results.copy()
plot_df["label"] = plot_df["driver"].map(LABELS)
plot_df["shapley_pct"] = plot_df["shapley"] / plot_df["shapley"].sum() * 100
plot_df["drop_one_pct"] = plot_df["drop_one"] / plot_df["drop_one"].sum() * 100
plot_df = plot_df.sort_values("shapley_pct", ascending=True)

methods = [
    ("drop_one_pct", "Drop-one"),
    ("shapley_pct", "Shapley"),
    ("johnson_pct", "Johnson RW"),
    ("rf_gini_pct", "RF Gini"),
]

fig_methods = go.Figure()
for color, (col, name) in zip(PALETTE, methods):
    fig_methods.add_trace(go.Bar(
        y=plot_df["label"],
        x=plot_df[col],
        name=name,
        orientation="h",
        marker_color=color,
        opacity=0.92,
        hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>%{fullData.name}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>",
    ))

fig_methods.update_layout(
    title="Driver rankings agree more than they disagree",
    barmode="group",
    xaxis_title="Share of total importance (%)",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=70, b=40),
    height=460,
)
show_plotly(
    fig_methods,
    caption="Normalized importance shares across four ranking methods (higher = stronger driver).",
)
```

### Correlation structure

Look at the off-diagonal cells — almost everything is positively correlated with everything else. If someone agrees the brand is trustworthy, they probably also agree it has good service, appealing design, social impact, the works. That clustering is exactly why a simple correlation ranking can lie to you. **Popularity** looks decent in isolation; it is much less special once the other attributes enter the model.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlations among drivers and satisfaction. Darker red = stronger positive association."

heat_cols = [OUTCOME] + DRIVERS
heat_labels = ["Satisfaction"] + [LABELS[d] for d in DRIVERS]
corr_heat = df[heat_cols].corr()
corr_heat.index = heat_labels
corr_heat.columns = heat_labels

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.8, 6.8), dpi=140)
im = ax.imshow(corr_heat, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-0.2, vmax=1.0, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(heat_labels)))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(heat_labels)))
ax.set_xticklabels(heat_labels, rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticklabels(heat_labels)
ax.set_title("Drivers move together — multicollinearity is real")

for i in range(len(heat_labels)):
    for j in range(len(heat_labels)):
        val = corr_heat.iloc[i, j]
        color = "#f0ece4" if abs(val) > 0.45 else ACCENT
        ax.text(j, i, f"{val:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=color)

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.02)
cbar.ax.tick_params(colors="#8a8278")
fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Bivariate vs. model-adjusted importance

This is my favorite chart. The dashed line is parity: same importance bivariate and multivariate. Points **below** the line looked better alone than they do in the full model — popularity and rewarding experience fall here. Points **above** it gain punch once everything else is controlled for — social impact is the clearest example. That gap between alone and adjusted is the whole multicollinearity lesson in one picture.

```{python}

scatter_df["label"] = scatter_df["driver"].map(LABELS)

        "<b>%{text}</b><br>"
        "Pearson r: %{x:.3f}<br>"
        "Std β: %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"
    ),
))
fig_scatter.add_shape(
    type="line",
    x0=0, y0=0, x1=lim, y1=lim,
    line=dict(color=GRID, width=1.5, dash="dash"),
)
fig_scatter.update_layout(
    title="What looks important alone vs. in the full model",
    xaxis_title="Pearson r with satisfaction",
    yaxis_title="Standardized β in full model",
    xaxis=dict(range=[0, lim]),
    yaxis=dict(range=[0, lim]),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=50),
    height=460,
    showlegend=False,
)
show_plotly(
    fig_scatter,
    caption="Pearson r (bivariate) vs. standardized β (multivariate). Points below the line lose importance after controls.",
)
```

## What surprised me

I expected more disagreement across methods. Instead, the ranking is stubbornly consistent:

- **Social impact** and **trust** top the decomposition methods (~20–22% of explained variance each). They also take the biggest hits in drop-one usefulness — remove either one and $R^2$ actually moves.
- **Customer service** is a solid third (~17%). Not flashy, but steady across Shapley, Johnson, and the forest.
- **Popularity** and **rewarding experience** are the fakers. Respectable Pearson correlations, weak everything else. They are riding coattails.

The random forest tells roughly the same story but spreads credit more evenly — build quality and rewarding experience pick up importance that the linear model does not give them. Trees are picking up something (maybe interactions), but they are not overturning the top three.

The sanity check I liked: **Shapley and Johnson weights nearly match row for row**, and both sum to $R^2$. When two completely different decompositions agree, I trust the ranking more than any single column in the table.

## What I’d actually recommend

If this were a real brand tracker — not a classroom dataset — I would tell the client to focus on **trust, social impact, and customer service** first. Not because one method said so, but because six methods pointed the same direction.

| Method | What it tells you | When it misleads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pearson *r* | Simple bivariate link | When drivers correlate (here: always) |
| Std β | Marginal effect in the full model | Same collinearity problem, different flavor |
| Drop-one | What you lose by removing a variable | Can feel punitive to correlated drivers |
| Shapley | Fair average share of $R^2$ | Slow with many predictors; assumes linearity |
| Johnson RW | Fast orthogonalized $R^2$ shares | Less intuitive behind the scenes |
| RF Gini | Nonlinear split importance | Different scale; not a causal claim |

Would I run all six every time? Probably not in production — Johnson or Shapley plus a correlation heatmap would be my default. But for learning why marketing analytics nerds distrust raw correlations, this dataset is a great toy.
